You're here. Good. Two pieces hold up everything that comes after — pay attention to them now and you won't have to come back here.

A **variable** is a name that holds a value. A **function** takes values, does a calculation and **returns** the result with `return`. Without `return`, it hands back `None` — in other words, nothing.

```python

price = 0.002          # float: a number with decimals

def add(a, b):         # a and b are the values coming in
    total = a + b      # + adds, - subtracts, * multiplies, / divides
    return total       # this is what leaves the function
```

In the exercises the `def` line is already written: you write the body. That `...` in the middle of the code is just a "write here" placeholder — delete it and put your code in its place.

By the end of this game you'll build an entire RAG system on your own. It starts here: adding up tokens.

exercicios.explicacao_md:
Python's most famous gotcha: the **mutable default**.

```python
def add(x, items=[]):       # [] is created ONCE, when the def runs
    items.append(x)
    return items

add(1)                      # [1]
add(2)                      # [1, 2]  <- the SAME list!

def add_ok(x, items=None):  # the fix: a None sentinel
    if items is None:
        items = []          # a new list on EVERY call
    items.append(x)
    return items
```

The default is evaluated only once, at definition time — every call without the argument shares the same object. In a chatbot, that turns into one user reading another user's history.

Another scoping rule in this tier: an inner function can see the outer function's variables (a closure), but to REASSIGN them it has to declare them `nonlocal`.
